focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to literature

outcomes.description: analyses representations of ideas in literature through narrative, character, imagery, symbol and connotation, and adapts these representations when creating texts
analyses representations of ideas in literature through genre and theme that reflect perspective and context, argument and authority, and adapts these representations when creating texts

items.text: Describe how narrative conventions engage the reader through models of behaviour, and apply narrative conventions when creating texts
items.examples: A moral or lesson of behaviour is woven into the narrative in a picture book, such as a fable. The behaviour is often explicitly formulated at the end, as in, ‘Slow and steady wins the race’.

items.text: Recognise that narratives reflect both personal and common lived experiences and offer models of behaviour, which may be rejected or accepted
items.examples: Aboriginal Dreaming stories may be told to share common experiences, share knowledge, clarify personal experience, tell history of Communities and/or connection to Country.

items.text: Describe how patterns in narratives set up expectations and notice when those patterns are subverted
items.examples: Quest narratives can portray an individual who overcomes their personal fears throughout the adventure, demonstrating the common need for perseverance.

items.text: Describe the difference in purpose between Aboriginal Dreaming stories and Aboriginal Songlines
items.examples:
Aboriginal Dreamings are stories that share cultural knowledges about creation, ways of doing, being and belonging.

Aboriginal Songlines describe landscapes and directions of travel of the tracks forged in land, sea and sky by Creator Spirits during the Dreaming.

items.text: Analyse attributes of character and use similar attributes when creating texts
items.examples: Attributes may include how real and imagined characters resemble the way people act, think, feel and communicate.

items.text: Recognise how character archetypes and stereotypes are represented in literature
items.examples: Archetypes and stereotypes may include real or imagined heroes, rebels or caregivers.

items.text: Analyse how engagement with characters within and between texts invites enjoyment of literature
items.examples:
Empathising with a character or caring about what happens to a character.

Enjoying identifying how they are similar to or different from a character.

items.text: Identify the ways different elements of a text contribute to character development and adapt these elements when creating texts
items.examples: The complex interrelationship of appearances, actions, attitudes and beliefs in a given context: The house a character lives in may be a manifestation of their character traits.

items.text: Analyse how figurative language in literature can enhance meaning and affect the audience
Recognise recurring and universal symbols and imagery in literature, describe their meanings and experiment with symbol and imagery when creating texts
items.examples: Archetypal heroes may be identified by a symbol.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors use symbols and imagery to share cultural perspectives and stories in texts
items.examples:
'Having a yarn up' could mean a gathering or meeting.

Creation represented by the Rainbow Serpent or Biame.

items.text: Explain how genre can be recognised by established codes and conventions that govern content and construction of literature, and apply this knowledge when creating texts
Examine and experiment with elements in literature that do not follow the form and function of a single genre
items.examples:
An adventure story may also be represented as science fiction.

A documentary may also be represented as a narrative.

items.text: Identify core social, personal and moral messages within and between texts
Identify and describe messages common to lived experiences that recur in literature and use these representations when creating texts
items.examples: Persistence and resilience can help one to overcome adversity and grow.

items.text: Identify how perspective is made evident through authorial choices
items.examples: This may include subject matter, structural arrangement, audience positioning, characterisation, language and style.

items.text: Explore how perspective is influenced by personal, social and cultural contexts
items.examples: Context can change the perspective: the context of a reader may differ from the context of a writer, the context of the past may differ from the present.

items.text: Describe how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors’ language use promotes a shared understanding of cultural context
items.examples: Specific elements of language can create a shared meaning across cultures, such as the use of ‘Aunty’ or ‘Uncle’, which might symbolise biological connections or someone important and respected.

items.text: Reflect on and explain how personal, social and cultural context is expressed in own texts
Recognise how an argument is influenced by perspective and create texts that adopt a perspective beyond personal experience
Understand the authority given to objectivity versus subjectivity in arguments
items.examples: Identifying the credibility of information expressed through supported arguments.

items.text: Analyse and compare features within and between texts, that characterise an authoritative style
items.examples: Textual features might include consistent genre, themes, point of view, visual elements or language devices across an author’s and illustrator’s published texts.

items.text: Compare the reliability and validity of texts to make judgements about their authority

focusAreas.title: Spelling

outcomes.description: automatically applies taught phonological, orthographic and morphological generalisations and strategies when spelling in a range of contexts, and justifies spelling strategies used to spell unfamiliar words

items.text: Segment unfamiliar multisyllabic words into syllables and phonemes as a strategy when spelling
items.examples: The word ‘recognise’ has 3 syllables and 8 phonemes.

items.text: Apply and explain graphemes identified by their etymology
items.examples:
The grapheme representing the final phoneme in repertoire reflects its French origin.

The grapheme representing the initial phoneme in pneumonia reflects its Greek origin.

items.text: Apply infrequently occurring graphemes and letter patterns when spelling base words in a range of writing contexts
items.examples: Such as bt in debt, ti in lotion, mb in climb and mn in column.

items.text: Recognise that the same grapheme can represent different phonemes
items.examples: The grapheme ei represents different phonemes in rein, protein, and feisty.

items.text: Proofread written texts to correct misspellings, making use of spelling reference tools where required
Explain and use spelling conventions to add derivational suffixes such as -ion, -ian, -ence, -ous to base words or roots
items.examples: The verb form to correct can be affixed to the suffix -ion to form an abstract noun, correction. No change to the base word, correct, is needed because it ends in ct.

items.text: Explain and use spelling conventions for assimilated prefixes such as in-, ad-, com-
items.examples: The final letter of some prefixes can be absorbed into the base or root by replacing the last letter of the prefix with the first letter of the base or root, resulting in a doubling of that letter (eg in + logical = illogical; ad + claim = acclaim; com + league = colleague).

items.text: Explain the etymology of taught roots and apply this knowledge when creating written texts
items.examples: A Greek root is chlor-, meaning green, in words such as chlorine, chloric and chlorophyll. A Latin root is audi-, meaning hearing or sound, in words such as audible, auditory and audition.

items.text: Correctly spell taught homophones when creating written texts across a range of writing topics and learning areas
items.examples: Tier 2 and Tier 3 homophones may be taught to expand both vocabulary knowledge and spelling. These might include torque and talk, and cell and sell.

focusAreas.title: Handwriting and digital transcription

outcomes.description: sustains a legible, fluent and automatic handwriting style
selects digital technologies to suit audience and purpose to create texts

items.text: Sustain writing with a legible, fluent and personal handwriting style across a text
Use handwriting efficiently in formal and informal situations
items.examples: Writing a formal persuasive letter to the principal or making informal notes when researching a topic.

items.text: Adjust handwriting style to suit writing purpose
Navigate the keyboard with efficiency and accuracy when typing words, numerals, punctuation and other symbols
Understand that the position of the device in relation to the user can affect posture and glare
Reflect on and monitor typing accuracy and rate according to goals and given criteria
Evaluate and select applications and tools to create text to suit audience and purpose
items.examples:
Word-processing software.

Speech-to-text and text-to-speech software.

Audio or video recording software.

Presentation software.

items.text: Use taught shortcut functions on digital tools to facilitate text creation

focusAreas.title: Oral language and communication

outcomes.description: communicates to wide audiences with social and cultural awareness, by interacting and presenting, and by analysing and evaluating for understanding

items.text: Initiate and contribute to sustained discussions, through questioning, building on and evaluating shared information
items.examples: Sustained discussion includes staying on topic, examining ideas and developing and supporting arguments.

items.text: Identify varying social conventions that influence interactions across wide audiences
Describe ways of interacting with cultural protocols or practices used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
items.examples:
Use of silence, gestures and hand talk during conversation.

Terms of respect – Aunty, Uncle.

Use of Aboriginal English or Aboriginal Language words.

Walking Country and the sharing of stories.

items.text: Follow agreed-upon protocols and define individual roles as needed for in-person or online interactions, establishing specific goals, criteria or timeframes
items.examples: Use of language that signals the roles of the chairperson and the different speaker positions in a classroom or inter-school debate.

items.text: Interact in a range of contexts and deliberately adjust language and style
items.examples:
Deliberate use of colloquialism, slang and jargon may be appropriate when interacting in an informal context.

Use of third-person point of view and minimal use of contractions may be appropriate when interacting in a formal context.

items.text: Ask and respond to analytical and evaluative questions about literature that contribute to own or others’ enjoyment and understanding
Evaluate the role of gesture during social and learning interactions and describe its impact on the audience
Respond to questions with elaboration and detail
Apply interactive listening strategies by responding to and providing feedback to the speaker
items.examples:
Giving the speaker undivided attention and acknowledging their message.

Deferring judgement.

Asking clarifying questions.

items.text: Apply active listening strategies by retelling or repeating what another person has expressed and by building on what has been said
Analyse key ideas and perspectives expressed by others through paraphrasing and note-taking
items.examples: Ideas may be received from a text read aloud or through diverse media, such as podcasts and audio books.

items.text: Analyse how audio elements in texts integrate with linguistic, visual, gestural and spatial elements to create meaning and impact
items.examples: Comparing and appraising the effectiveness of the integration of elements, such as sound effects, images, gestures, positioning and lighting.

items.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of rhetorical questions used for intentional effect
items.examples:
Evaluative questioning may include:
Does the author’s rhetorical question persuade me to agree with their point of view?
Does the author’s rhetorical question encourage me to act or respond in a certain way?
Does the abundance of rhetorical questions by the author weaken their effect?

items.text: Evaluate features of spoken texts that contribute to own or others’ enjoyment
Deliver presentations suited to purpose and audience
items.examples: Moderating length, content and style of delivery.

items.text: Experiment with volume, pace and intonation to enhance meaning when presenting and reciting, and recognise the effects these have on audience understanding
Select and use a variety of sentence lengths to suit the purpose of planned spoken texts
Use connectives to signal a change in perspective or to show causal relationships when speaking
items.examples:
Connectives that signal a change include however, although and on the other hand.

Connectives that show causal relationships include due to and since.

items.text: Use expanded noun and verb groups to present planned, detailed descriptions
items.examples:
Expanded noun group: The mighty and meandering Murray River is the longest river in Australia.

Expanded verb group: Construction of the building will be completed in the next year.

items.text: Present multimodal arguments that include research and references, topic-specific vocabulary and the selection of persuasive techniques appropriate to audience
items.examples: This could include presenting arguments in a debate in class or with another school.

items.text: Select multimedia components, visual displays or use gestural features to enhance and bring clarity to presentations
items.examples: Multimedia components may include graphics, images, music and sounds. Gestural features may include hand actions, eye contact and facial expressions.

items.text: Reflect on and monitor own and peer presentations according to given criteria

focusAreas.title: Creating written texts

outcomes.description: plans, creates and revises written texts for multiple purposes and audiences through selection of text features, sentence-level grammar, punctuation and word-level language

items.text: Choose literary forms with appropriate text structures, features and language to engage target audiences
items.examples:
Choose to present a literary text in the form of a poem, rather than a short story.

In a short story, disrupt the linear narrative sequence with a memory, flashback or time leap.

In a poem, such as in shape poetry or in free verse, innovate on layouts that represent a theme or topic, or guide navigation for the reader.

items.text: Make creative choices about temporal and spatial settings, character profiles and motives to enhance reader engagement
items.examples: Students select a time and place that furthers the idea or theme they are exploring, such as in a story about the desire for freedom that may be set in a time and place of oppression.

items.text: Experiment with characterisation
items.examples: Challenge stereotypes such as an older person must be wise, a clown is always funny.

items.text: Choose and control narrative voice across a text
items.examples: Narrative voices are: first voice – I travelled on the train; second voice – you travelled on the train; third voice – Pierre travelled on the train.

items.text: Experiment with the development of thematic elements
items.examples: In a fairy tale identified themes may include good vs evil, courage in the face of adversity.

items.text: Select and use poetic forms to descriptively express ideas
items.examples: Free verse, limerick, cinquain, haiku, concrete (shape poem) and sonnet.

items.text: Choose text formats with appropriate text structures, features and language to inform target audiences
items.examples:
Text structures and features may differ for:
Cause-and-effect explanations, that may include flowcharts to explain interrelationships.
Instructions, that may include annotated images to show steps.
Descriptions, that may include class and sub-class relationships.

items.text: Develop informative texts that include headings, ideas grouped into paragraphs that include a topic sentence, and a paragraph with concluding information
Describe and/or explain ideas through logically sequenced paragraphs
Compare and contrast or discuss cause and effect through sequenced paragraphs
Create factual and historical accounts that incorporate broader contextual information
items.examples: Explore sustainable practices used within the school, the local community and the world.

items.text: Choose text formats with appropriate text structures, features and language to persuade a target audience
items.examples: Text structures, features and language will differ for letters, reviews, editorials, advertisements, articles and written speeches.

items.text: Group ideas to develop a statement of position, and clear, logical lines of argument that synthesise points, and structure a rhetorically effective conclusion
Create objective, impersonal arguments
Combine personal and objective arguments for persuasive effect
items.examples: Moderate first person when stating a personal opinion by using third person to state facts.

items.text: Present arguments from one or multiple viewpoints to persuade target audiences
Use rhetorical devices targeted to the audience
Use modality to qualify or strengthen arguments
Control tense across a text according to purpose, shifting between past, present and future tense if required
items.examples:
Informative texts can use timeless present tense such as, ‘A kangaroo is a marsupial.’

An information text can shift between tense such as, ‘Historically, dogs were used (past) for hunting and protective purposes. Now, dogs are (present) also valued for their companionship, evidenced by the fact that more than half of NSW households own a domestic dog. According to scientists, technology is advancing (continuous present) so rapidly, dog-to-human communication will (future) soon be a reality between you and your pooch.’

items.text: Maintain correct noun–pronoun referencing, subject–verb agreement and use temporal, conditional and causal connectives to build cohesive links across a text
Use word repetition and word associations as cohesive devices across texts
Substitute specific nouns with all-purpose words as a cohesive device to replace verb groups, noun groups or whole clauses
items.examples: We’ve got 2 cars. You can use one – cars is substituted with one.

items.text: Experiment with figurative language for effect and to engage the reader, including metaphor, hyperbole, oxymoron and allusion
Create written texts that include multiple paragraphs with clear, coherent transition of ideas
Choose multimodal features suited to a target audience and purpose, to reinforce and extend ideas
items.examples: Use graphs, tables and images that represent data and ideas.

items.text: Acknowledge sources of information to add credibility and authority to arguments and information
items.examples:
According to…’ – ‘As described by…’

‘XX stated that…’

items.text: Experiment with the use of non-finite verbs in adverbial clauses
items.examples:
In an imaginative text: ‘After eating lunch, the giant stomped through the misty forest.’

In an informative text: ‘Being an endangered species, Tasmanian devils are protected in national parks.’

In a persuasive text: ‘To ensure a bountiful harvest, we must pick the fruit.’

items.text: Make choices about verbs and verb groups to achieve precision and add detail
items.examples: Select ‘The giant exploded in laughter’, instead of, ‘The giant laughed loudly.’

items.text: Experiment with embedding adjectival clauses with the subject and/or object of other clauses, to modify the meaning or to add detail to a noun or noun group
items.examples:
In an imaginative text: ‘Living harmoniously in the lush valley, the fairies love to dance,’ might change to include an embedded clause: ‘The fairies, who live harmoniously in the lush valley, love to dance.’

In an informative text: ‘Deep-fried food is not healthy, but many people love it,’ might change to include an embedded clause: ‘Deep-fried food, which many people love, is not healthy.’

In a persuasive text: ‘The small and obscure park near the beach is an exceptional attraction for family gatherings,’ might change to include an embedded clause: ‘The park near the beach, which is small and obscure, is an exceptional attraction for family gatherings.’

items.text: Experiment with the placement of adverbial clauses, to modify the meaning or to add detail to a verb or verb group
items.examples:
In an imaginative text: ‘After the sun went down, the old house came to life’ might change with the placement of the adverbial clause: ‘The old house came to life after the sun went down.’

In an informative text: ‘Wombats are called nocturnal because they forage and feed at night’ might change with the placement of the adverbial clause: ‘Because they forage and feed at night, wombats are called nocturnal.’

In a persuasive text: ‘We could improve our park if we raised funds for a new slide’ might change with the placement of the adverbial clause: ‘If we raised funds for a new slide, we could improve our park.’

items.text: Include appositives to provide details to nouns and to vary sentence structures suited to text purpose
items.examples:
An appositive is a noun, pronoun or noun group, often including modifiers, positioned beside another noun or pronoun to describe or identify it. Such as for:

An imaginative purpose: ‘Loreta, my long-time and loyal friend, was waiting for me at the train station when the celebrations started.’
An informative purpose: 'The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, is located off the coast of Queensland.'
A persuasive purpose: ‘Worm farms, or compost bins, keep food waste out of landfill.’

items.text: Create nominalisations to convey abstract ideas and concepts succinctly and authoritatively
items.examples: Use nominalisation in an informative text, such as: ‘Air pollution is a problem’, instead of, ‘It is a problem if we pollute the air’.

items.text: Make choices about the use of declarative, exclamatory, interrogative and imperative sentences to suit text purpose, and for meaning and effect
items.examples:
Declarative sentence to present facts or evidence: ‘Regular exercise is recommended for a healthy lifestyle.’

Exclamatory sentence to express strong emotion: ‘Evacuate! Get out now!’

Interrogative sentence for rhetorical effect: ‘Where would you be without us?’

Imperative sentence to provide instructions: ‘Save your work before you log out.’

items.text: Vary sentence structures or lengths when using simple, compound and complex sentences, with a focus on achieving clarity and effect suited to text purpose
items.examples:
Use short sentences to build tension or for clarity when explaining dense or technical information.

Use complex sentences to expand on what is happening in the main clause or other adverbial clauses.

items.text: Use capital letters at the beginning of a sentence, to indicate proper nouns, for headings and subheadings, to indicate the beginning of a poetry line, for emphasis, and when using acronyms
items.examples:
Capitalisation for emphasis may be suitable as a persuasive or expressive device, such as ‘SALE on now!’, or ‘BANG!’ went the door.

At the beginning of traditional poetry lines.

items.text: Use a comma to separate a subordinate clause or a phrase from the main clause, or to separate information within a sentence, or to separate items in a list
items.examples:
Separate the subordinate clause from the main clause with a comma, when it is positioned before the main clause: When assembling new furniture, you should first read the instructions.

Separate information displayed in parentheses: The lion was patiently stalking its prey (an innocent young antelope), slowly moving closer and closer.

Separate items in a list: You will need a hammer, screwdriver, spanner and saw.

items.text: Use quotation marks consistently across a text to distinguish words that are spoken by characters in dialogue or words authored by others
Understand that texts, such as poetry, may include innovative use of punctuation, and experiment with punctuation to suit purpose and for effect
Use parentheses in the first instance when abbreviating names using acronyms, and when acknowledging a source
items.examples:
The World Health Organization (WHO) works to promote health and safety for all people.

The latest survey results showed … (enter name, date of information source).

items.text: Experiment with dashes and parentheses for humorous or ironic effect
Understand and use simple hyphenation generalisations
items.examples:
Use a hyphen at a line break when a word cannot fit on one line, but not if the word is less than 6 letters, or less than 2-syllables. At the end of a line, a hyphen can be used to break a word between syllables or morphemes: data-base, re-cover, diction-ary.

When writing fractions, such as two-thirds, and numbers between twenty-one and ninety-nine.

items.text: Use topic-specific Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary intentionally to add credibility and enhance authority
items.examples: In an informative text focused on space exploration, terms such as planetary, galaxy, astronaut and cosmos might be used.

items.text: Experiment with word choices to create humour, for clarity or emphasis, to suit audience and purpose
Control modality related to probability, occurrence, obligation or inclination for precision
items.examples:
Intensify or soften emotional responses: can laugh, may laugh, might laugh, should laugh.

Modal words can indicate probability (might, perhaps), occurrence (regularly, rarely), obligation (must, ought) and inclination (desire).

items.text: Select and use a range of synonyms in a longer text, for precision and to create variety for reader engagement
Select text formats for combined purposes, creating hybrid texts for target audiences
Use print or digital tools to plan, sequence, create, revise, edit and publish texts
Research and summarise information from several sources to plan for writing
Create texts using digital technologies suited to a target audience and purpose, to support and enhance the development of ideas
Assess the reliability and authority of sources, including digital sources, when researching and acknowledging texts
Reflect on own writing by explaining and justifying authorial decisions regarding text-level features, sentence-level grammar, punctuation and word-level language
Re-read, proofread and edit own and other’s writing, and use criteria and goals in response to feedback
items.examples: Criteria for revisions may include refining or expanding ideas, improving text cohesion, using more appropriate or effective words and ensuring correct spelling is evident.

focusAreas.title: Vocabulary

outcomes.description: extends Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary through interacting, wide reading and writing, morphological analysis and generating precise definitions for specific contexts

items.text: Identify newly encountered words from interactions and wide reading, and use them in writing, discussions and presentations
Identify and use words that convey informative and objective meanings in texts
Identify and use words that convey subjective, emotive and persuasive meanings in texts
Use metalanguage when discussing language features encountered in texts
Extend knowledge of literal and non-literal word meanings through idiom or metaphor
items.examples:
The word moon has a non-literal meaning in the idiom, over the moon, to infer an emotional state.

The metaphor the snow is a white blanket alludes to something soft in its comparison of snow to a blanket.

items.text: Apply knowledge of taught Tier 3 subject-specific morphemes and their meanings
items.examples: The morpheme dec, deca or deci means ‘10’ and micro means ‘small in size or extent’.

items.text: Identify Aboriginal English words used in multimodal, spoken and written texts
items.examples:
Gammon: joking or pretending.

Mob: family or group.

Deadly: awesome.

Tidda: sister or close female connection.

items.text: Identify and use words derived from other languages, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages, and know that the pronunciation and spelling of words may reflect their etymology
items.examples:
Kangaroo reflects the Guugu Yimidhirr word gangurru.

Koala and kurrajong are from the Dharug language.

Quandong is from the Wiradjuri language.

Repertoire is from the French language.

Pneumonia is from the Greek language.

Pretzel is from the German language.

items.text: Describe multiple meanings of words, including their metaphorical uses
items.examples: The word elephant refers to an animal; however, the phrase the elephant in the room refers to the subject that no one wants to discuss.

items.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of modal words used in texts to intensify or soften emotional responses
items.examples: Comparing which word is more effective in these sentences: ‘The long drought seemed endless’, or ‘The devastating drought seemed endless’.

items.text: Analyse morphemic structures of Tier 2 and Tier 3 words to determine their meaning
Compare nuances and subtleties between synonyms to discern the most appropriate word for a given context
items.examples: Comparing words such as ability or capacity and abstain or refrain.

focusAreas.title: Reading comprehension

outcomes.description: fluently reads and comprehends texts for wide purposes, analysing text structures and language, and by monitoring comprehension

items.text: Syllabify, blend grapheme–phoneme correspondences and use morphemic knowledge as strategies for reading words accurately
Adjust reading rate to suit the purpose for reading and the complexity of the text
items.examples: Read quickly to skim or scan for information; read slowly with pauses to synthesise information and make notes; read at a leisurely or conversational pace for enjoyment.

items.text: Adjust prosodic reading to enhance meaning and engage an audience
Efficiently follow signposting features to navigate print and digital texts
items.examples: Signposting features could include headings and sub-headings, homepages and subpages, hyperlinks and hypertext.

contentGroups.title: Reading for interest and wide purposes

items.text: Select, compare and reflect on texts read for personal interest
items.examples: Broaden or deepen understanding and empathy.

items.text: Reflect on reading experiences and identify texts and language features that are enjoyable
Select texts from print or digital sources to gather and organise research on a topic
Use criteria to determine the accuracy and reliability of sourced information
items.examples: Information that is credible and reliable helps to determine the authority of a text.

items.text: Adjust reading approach to suit the purpose for reading
items.examples: Close reading for analysis, skimming for key information, scanning for key vocabulary, note-taking for summarisation, reading for enjoyment.

items.text: Bring subject vocabulary, technical vocabulary, background knowledge and conceptual knowledge to new reading tasks
Compare and evaluate print and digital texts for their pertinence to a task, their authority and their level of detail
Use and compare different texts on similar themes or topics to synthesise ideas or information
Use knowledge of text structure to navigate the text to locate specific information
Analyse how the integration of persuasive, informative and/or narrative structures within a text can enhance effect
Compare purposes for different texts and consider why authors and illustrators have structured texts in particular ways
Analyse use of multimodal features to enhance meaning within texts
items.examples:
Explaining and interpreting the use of visual, audio, gestural and spatial features in texts.

Exploring salience and the effect of choices regarding the framing of an image and placement of elements in the image.

items.text: Use morphology and etymology to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words
Describe how own mental model is adjusted as new words and information deepen understanding during reading
items.examples: A flashback to the characters’ initial encounters in a text, may provide reasons for the tension between the characters.

items.text: Explain how language evokes responses when reading
items.examples: ‘I love this house’ can evoke the judgement that a house is lovable.

items.text: Explain how modality can have subtle impacts on the meanings of words and contribute to deeper understanding when reading
items.examples: This can include modal verbs that express attitudes of obligation or certainty, such as might and must, or words that give greater impact, such as worried and frantic.

items.text: Identify lexical cohesive devices used by the author that support understanding when reading
items.examples: Lexical devices may include synonyms, hypernyms, whole and part word associations (such as some picnic supplies, one of which is bread).

items.text: Recognise that anaphors, such as pronouns and verb groups, take their meanings from other parts of a text to support inference
items.examples: In the sentence, ‘He won’t play another game of soccer, but she will …’, the anaphor is that ‘she will’ play another game of soccer.

items.text: Identify cause and effect, using knowledge of causal connectives
items.examples: In consequence, so, because.

items.text: Understand that sentence openers signal what the sentence will be about, and that the rest of the sentence can provide new information
Analyse how the meanings of key words and phrases in sentences and across a text support local and global inferencing when reading
items.examples:
Local inference may occur by identifying word associations across consecutive sentences: ‘Look at those apples. Fujis are my favourite.’ The inference is that Fujis are apples.

Global inferences may occur by linking the meaning of key words across larger sections of a text.

items.text: Recognise that personal narratives contain more subjective language, but factual accounts of events contain more objective language
Compare and evaluate subjective and objective language to identify bias
items.examples:
Subjective language: spiders are scary.

Objective language: spiders have 8 legs.

items.text: Recognise that a sequence of clauses may use different tenses but remains connected throughout a topic or section of text
items.examples: As Ruby sailed, thoughts of friends and family washed over her like the surge of the sea washing over the deck of the boat.

items.text: Analyse how language, background and vocabulary knowledge, and inferencing are used together to effectively build and adjust a mental model prior to and during reading
items.examples:
Background knowledge can include a student’s prior knowledge or knowledge specifically built around a topic before reading.

Vocabulary could include Tier 2 and Tier 3 words that may relate to a topic and may be encountered in a text.

Inferences could derive from known authors and illustrators and topic knowledge, and text features such as title, images or graphics, table of contents, headings and subheadings.

items.text: Monitor and repair reading when meaning breaks down
items.examples: This might include pausing, self-correcting, re-reading or reading on; using phonic, morphemic and word knowledge; and reactivating background knowledge.

items.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of comprehension strategies used to support reading and interpretation of texts
items.examples: Strategies might include predicting, inferring, making connections, summarising, synthesising and evaluating.

items.text: Ask questions to clarify thinking, and to provide reasons or evidence
Question the assertions made by authors when engaging with print and digital texts

items.text: Recount stories or personal experiences
items.examples:
Using icons for who, what, when and where to support the recounting of a personal narrative, or the retelling of a story.

Recounting a story read in class.

Describing an event that happened, including a beginning, middle and end.

items.text: Respond imaginatively to a written or multimodal text
items.examples:
Creating a song or picture in response to a text.

Creating an alternative ending to a film or creating an additional scene or slide.

Creating a presentation or performance.

items.text: Create mood or tone using vocabulary and/or language features
items.examples:
Choosing descriptive vocabulary.

Using figurative language.

items.text: Compose, informative, persuasive, analytical or imaginative texts in response to a text
items.examples:
Creating a review for a film viewed in class.

Creating a digital or poster presentation to summarise a topic.

Creating a diary entry from the perspective of a character in a narrative.

items.text: Compose texts using language forms, features or structures to communicate with or engage an audience
items.examples:
Using humour to engage an audience.

Using past or present tense, or first-person or third-person voice to position the audience.

Using digital technology to express personal style in a presentation.

items.text: Select and use a range of modes, media or technology to represent ideas
items.examples:
Creating a poster to demonstrate their opinion about a theme.

Creating a presentation to depict or sequence a familiar event.

items.text: Create a visual or multimodal text to convey a message
items.examples:
Selecting an image to represent a request, feeling or opinion.

Creating a visual display about a theme or experience.

items.text: Combine visual and language features to create texts
items.examples:
Creating an online profile.

Creating a poster to advertise an event.

Creating an infographic, brochure or information report.

items.text: Combine visual and language features to create mood or tone
items.examples:
Selecting colours, fonts and graphics.

Choosing vocabulary.

items.text: Communicate a personal experience or idea
Recognise how nonverbal language can support or enhance meaning in spoken texts
items.examples:
Identifying a speaker’s use of gesture in a dialogue and what it means.

Recognising the tone and emphasis used by a speaker in presenting an argument.

items.text: Understand that intonation, pace and emphasis for clarity enhance meaning when delivering spoken texts
items.examples:
Emphasising different words in a sentence and discussing how this changes the meaning.

Observing how differences in pace impact the audience’s understanding of a spoken text.

items.text: Use language forms and features appropriate to spoken texts
items.examples:
Identifying where and when spoken texts are used.

Comparing spoken and written texts on the same topic.

Creating a speech that includes an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion.

items.text: Identify structures of informative, persuasive, analytical or imaginative texts
items.examples:
Acknowledging a complication in a narrative.

Placing a deconstructed text back into the correct order, giving reasons for placement choices.

Discussing where different structural points, such as the conclusion, are found in specific texts.

items.text: Use scaffolds to create informative, persuasive, analytical or imaginative texts
items.examples:
Using a scaffold with who, what and where to create a story.

Following a visual, such as a graphic organiser, to develop parts of a text.

Using a scaffold to develop an introduction for a speech or information report.

items.text: Sequence ideas when composing informative, persuasive, analytical or imaginative texts
Compose a text with a central idea
Explore different strategies, including writing conventions and processes, to enhance texts
items.examples:
Reviewing and amending vocabulary, spelling, punctuation or sentence structure using strategies that support writing.

Using graphic organisers, headings and tools to enhance cohesion in paragraphs and presentations.

items.text: Experiment with texts to develop creativity in writing
items.examples: Creating a collage of words or images that creatively convey a message or theme.

items.text: Create simple, compound or complex sentences to communicate a message
items.examples:
Selecting individual words to create a sentence.

Matching clauses to create a compound sentence.

Adding a clause into an existing sentence to compose a complex sentence.

items.text: Explore grammar conventions at sentence level
items.examples:
Identifying the tense used in a text.

Recognising tenses, adjectives, action verbs or cohesive links in texts.

Discussing how using different tenses, adjectives, action verbs or cohesive links can change the meaning in texts.

items.text: Apply grammar conventions to create accurate and logical sentences
items.examples:
Correcting inconsistent tense in a text.

Changing adjectives, action verbs or cohesive links in a sentence to change meaning.

items.text: Recognise the purpose of punctuation conventions
items.examples:
Discussing how punctuation changes meaning.

Correcting punctuation errors in a text.

items.text: Use punctuation conventions to create accurate and logical sentences
items.examples:
Beginning a sentence with a capital letter and ending a sentence with a full stop.

Using commas accurately to separate items in a list, or to signify a dependent clause.

items.text: Recognise spelling patterns in familiar words
items.examples: Identifying words that begin or end with the same digraph.

items.text: Engage phonological, orthographic or morphological strategies to spell unfamiliar or technical words
items.examples:
Identifying words that start or end with the same sound.

Breaking words into morphemes.

Using Auslan fingerspelling.

Identifying the same morphemes in different words.

Sounding out words by morphemes.

items.text: Use and extend familiar vocabulary to compose texts
items.examples:
Ranking synonyms in order of modality, such as nice, attractive, gorgeous, irresistible.

Creating word clouds, including synonyms, antonyms, verbs and nouns, from the same root or base word.

Creating or using a word bank when creating texts.

Using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems to communicate known and unfamiliar words to create texts.

items.text: Explore words with multiple meanings
items.examples: Recognising that the word orange can refer to the colour or the fruit, left can signify a direction or that somebody has gone; and park can mean a recreational area or what a driver does in a car park.

items.text: Consider personal experiences to select vocabulary to compose texts
items.examples: Creating a word bank to represent emotions experienced in a personal event and using this to reflect on the event.

items.text: Select topic-specific vocabulary to compose texts

focusAreas.title: Expressing ideas and composing texts A

outcomes.description: crafts personal, creative and critical texts for a range of audiences by experimenting with and controlling language forms and features to shape meaning

items.text: Select and adapt appropriate codes, conventions and structures to shape meaning when composing written texts that are analytical, informative, persuasive, discursive and/or imaginative
items.examples: Analysing literary devices and stylistic features of different forms, including the ways in which different structural choices influence meaning, by reading model texts.

items.text: Develop a personal and informed voice that generates ideas and positions an audience through selection of appropriate word-level language and text-level features
Experiment with language to create tone, atmosphere and mood
items.examples: Using expressive words that enhance tone, atmosphere and mood, such as vitriol, reticence and nonchalance.

items.text: Use rhetorical language strategically and subtly to shape complex ideas and convince others of a point of view, as appropriate to audience and purpose
items.examples:
Using irony or humour to communicate a serious aspect of topics.

Applying parody or ridicule to counteract opposing ideas.

items.text: Use tense accurately and purposefully
items.examples: Using a consistent and appropriate combination of past, present and future tenses, in imaginative and persuasive texts, for specific purposes.

items.text: Apply narrative voice to depict complex ideas and enhance engagement
items.examples: Experimenting with metafictional elements by shaping a second-person narrator.

items.text: Create engaging and authentic temporal and spatial settings for a range of purposes and audiences
items.examples: Shaping parallel narrative arcs that depict different time periods, settings or perspectives.

items.text: Experiment with a variety of codes and conventions to create aesthetic qualities that have the power to communicate ideas and influence viewpoints in own texts
items.examples:
Applying the elements of mise-en-scène, such as camera angles, lighting and symbolic props, to create tension.

Experimenting with textual form and hybridity to represent new or existing perspectives in engaging ways.

items.text: Compose visual and multimodal texts to express complex ideas, using a range of digital technologies where appropriate
Select effective rhetorical strategies to position an audience and evoke an emotional response
Communicate complex information, ideas and viewpoints using purposeful verbal and/or nonverbal language, including gestures, to emphasise key points, enhance engagement and clarify meaning
Craft a range of spoken, signed or communicated texts that convey complex ideas for specific audiences
Deliver spoken, signed or communicated texts with engaging use of intonation, emphasis, volume, pace and timing
Participate in and lead a range of informal discussions about texts and ideas, including analytical, speculative and exploratory talk, to consolidate personal understanding and generate new ideas
Signal the development of ideas through language, structure and presentational features
items.examples: Purposefully using opposition, reinforcement, illustration, emphasis, cause and effect, and time connectives.

items.text: Express ideas, using appropriate structures for purpose and audience, that reflect an emerging personal style
items.examples:
Examining how voice and tone are shaped in persuasive, discursive and reflective texts.

Experimenting with a blended objective and subjective voice, such as first and third-person voice.

items.text: Introduce and define complex key ideas, academic concepts and positions for arguments in sustained analytical and persuasive texts
items.examples: Using refined research skills to elicit appropriate source material to enhance own compositions.

items.text: Use the structural conventions of analytical writing purposefully, including a well-articulated and considered thesis, a sustained and cohesive progression of supporting points, and a rhetorically effective conclusion

Use the structural conventions of persuasive texts to purposefully justify opinions and develop expanding arguments, including a focused opening and thesis, logically sequenced elaboration paragraphs, and a conclusion that synthesises complex ideas
Use the structural conventions of informative texts purposefully to build a field of relevant facts and perspectives
Use the structural conventions of imaginative texts purposefully, including shaping complex complications and conflicts, and crafting authentic characters, to depict ideas
Experiment with the process of transformation to create texts with new meaning
Use the structural conventions of discursive texts purposefully, including the transition between personal and abstract texts, to present complex and nuanced ideas
items.examples: Offering a hypothetical to draw an analogy that engages the reader’s emotional response, before transitioning to a conceptual abstraction that challenges an idea.

items.text: Experiment with a range of poetic forms to explore ideas and express personal perspectives
items.examples: Playing with the ways slam poetry can prompt personal reflection.

items.text: Experiment with a combination of modes for specific effect and impact
items.examples: Choosing scenes from a film and changing the sound effects or musical choices to change the meaning.

items.text: Select and justify the use of varied sentence type, length and complexity to support cohesion and for effect
items.examples: Declarative, exclamatory, interrogative and imperative sentences that are crafted using simple, compound and complex structures.

items.text: Maintain subject–verb agreement, identifying the subject in collective nouns, extended noun groups or in extended complex sentences
Control the use of passive and active voice when crafting sentences for effect and to suit the purpose of a text
Craft concise sentences to suit text purpose
Craft elaborated noun and/or verb groups for effect, clarity or complexity of description
Apply punctuation to suit text purpose, support clarity and meaning, for effect, and to control reader response
Apply orthographic and morphological knowledge, using etymology and dictionary reference resources as needed, to spell unfamiliar, complex and technical words
items.examples: Referencing resources, such as print or digital sources, to locate and correctly spell Greek and Latin roots, prefixes, suffixes and homophones, including multimorphemic words, in meaningful contexts.

items.text: Select technical vocabulary to write with accuracy in a range of modes and registers appropriate to audience, purpose, form and context
Use a variety of grammatical features to describe relationships between complex ideas
Make vocabulary choices that enhance stylistic features of writing, and shape meaning through connotation
items.examples: Crafting descriptions that rely on indirect imagery and pathetic fallacy to suggest the emotions of characters.

focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to texts C

outcomes.description: makes connections with and between texts

items.text: Identify genres of texts
items.examples: Identifying the common elements of particular genres, such as heroes and villains in action/adventure texts, or close-up shots and emotive music in romance films.

items.text: Explore language, character archetypes and/or visuals in a genre
Communicate a preference for a particular genre
items.examples: Discussing the features of a genre that make it personally appealing.

items.text: Communicate connections between texts
items.examples:
Matching the meanings of signs, symbols or images to the ideas in texts.

Identifying or comparing characters in texts and how they act in certain ways.

Identifying when texts allude to other well-known texts.

items.text: Recognise that texts can be adapted for different audiences, purposes or contexts
items.examples:
Viewing the opening sequence of different adaptations of the same story and discussing the differences.

Exploring informal and formal language or features to express the same idea, such as a text message, email or letter.

items.text: Explore adaptations and/or appropriations of texts
items.examples: Viewing the film version of a written text and comparing similarities and differences.

items.text: Identify when a text has connections to other texts
items.examples: Identifying intertextual references in a poem or film.

items.text: Identify the ways that connections between texts create a richer meaning
items.examples: Discussing how a narrative can refer to another text and, in the process, add ideas from that text.

items.text: Identify a personal experience conveyed by a text
Explore how texts can represent significant personal experiences or ideas
items.examples:
Engaging with texts that explore shared experiences.

Identifying what a text can teach us about ourselves.

items.text: Explore texts from a range of cultures and storytellers, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures
items.examples: Exploring the impact of stories from a range of cultures and experiences, including why these stories are told.

focusAreas.title: Expressing ideas and composing texts B

outcomes.description: uses processes of planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting to purposefully develop and refine composition of texts

items.text: Engage with model texts to develop and refine features, structures and stylistic approaches in own work
Research, summarise, evaluate and synthesise information and perspectives from different sources to generate new ideas and create detailed and informed texts
Develop an effective thesis for extended analytical and persuasive texts that is based on critical thinking about a text or topic
items.examples: Drafting a series of increasingly detailed thesis sentences that aim to capture the central details of an argument, using nominalisations, verb groups and multiple clauses.

items.text: Plan a progressive sequence of arguments or ideas, and set goals at conceptual, whole text and paragraph levels
items.examples: Reviewing the scope of evidence used to argue each point in the sequence and identifying any gaps in the way knowledge of the topic or text is represented.

items.text: Produce co-constructed complex texts to represent a diversity of ideas and values
Select from a range of collaborative drafting strategies and feedback processes to improve clarity, meaning and effect in texts
items.examples: Providing practical feedback on other students’ drafts according to the criteria of a task and re-applying what they have learnt to improve their own work.

items.text: Reflect on own texts, using technical vocabulary to explain and evaluate authorial decisions appropriate to the target audience and specific purpose
Discuss the pleasures, challenges and successes experienced in the processes of understanding and composing
Evaluate the effectiveness of compositional choices in writing that have been influenced by elements of other texts, using specific examples
Evaluate own ability to plan, monitor and revise during the composition process, and how this can improve clarity, cohesion and effect

focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to texts A

outcomes.description: analyses how meaning is created through the use and interpretation of increasingly complex language forms, features and structures

items.text: Analyse how contextual, creative and unconscious influences shape the composition, understanding and interpretation of all representations
Use metalanguage effectively to analyse how meaning is constructed by linguistic and stylistic elements in texts

Analyse how language forms, features and structures, specific or conventional to a text’s medium, context, purpose and audience, shape meaning, and experiment with this understanding through written, spoken, visual and multimodal responses
items.examples: Considering how nonfiction texts draw on features and structures of fiction texts to engage readers and explore ideas.

items.text: Explain how texts use, adapt or subvert textual conventions across a range of modes and media to shape new meanings, and explore this in own texts
items.examples: Analysing how a digital narrative includes common structural and stylistic devices, such as viewpoint, characterisation and figurative language, to create an interactive narrative.

items.text: Analyse how figurative language and devices can be used to represent complex ideas, thoughts and feelings to contribute to larger patterns of meaning in texts, and experiment with this in own texts
items.examples: Analysing how devices, such as literary metaphor, motif and contrast can shape meaning throughout a text.

items.text: Analyse how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors use figurative language and devices to represent culture, identity and experience

Examine elements of focalisation, such as omniscience, limitations, indirect speech, tone, reliability and multiple narrators, and how these interact to shape perceptions of meaning in texts, and apply this in own texts
items.examples: Explaining how the experiences and thoughts of characters and personas are focalised in texts to shape how the reader interprets information, including the effects of narrative distance, limitations and (un)reliable narration.

items.text: Recognise the difference between the actual author and authorial voice in texts and use this understanding to create texts with other kinds of imagined authors
Analyse how engaging, dynamic and complex characters are constructed in texts using language features and structures, and use these features and structures in own texts
items.examples: Considering how characters can be indirectly constructed through elements of narrative point of view, such as focalisation and indirect speech.

items.text: Explore how characters in texts can be lifelike constructions with whom audiences establish intellectual and emotional connections, and can be perceived to reflect, challenge or subvert particular values and attitudes
Analyse how characters can serve structural roles in narrative, such as foils and drivers of action and conflict, and manipulate these ideas when composing own texts
Analyse how narrative conventions vary across genres, modes, media and contexts and how they can be used to represent ideas and values and shape responses, and apply this understanding in own texts
items.examples: Understanding how elements of narrative, such as orientation, may be abbreviated, omitted or implied by small details for effect.

items.text: Explore how narratives can represent and shape personal and shared identities, values and experiences
items.examples: Analysing how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors, and authors from a range of cultural backgrounds, choose to represent their identities and experiences through texts.

focusAreas.title: Reading, viewing and listening to texts

outcomes.description: uses a range of personal, creative and critical strategies to interpret complex texts

items.text: Apply reading pathways appropriate to form, purpose and meaning, and connect ideas within and between texts
items.examples: Reviewing elements of the text, such as the arrangement of words, both grammatically and syntactically, to understand linear and sequential text, such as in a novel, and nonlinear and non-sequential text, such as in a website.

items.text: Use contextual cues to infer the meaning of unfamiliar or complex words
Develop a deeper understanding of themes, ideas or attitudes by revisiting and reinterpreting texts to find new meaning

contentGroups.title: Reading, viewing and listening for meaning

items.text: Analyse the main ideas and thematic concerns represented in texts
items.examples: Understanding that texts present ambiguous and complex ethical issues that are more nuanced than simply right or wrong, and discussing personal responses to these human dilemmas.

items.text: Investigate how layers of meaning are constructed in texts and how this shapes a reader’s understanding and engagement
items.examples: Understanding and evaluating how certain stylistic choices, such as parallel or frame narratives, can create multiple layers of interpretation.

items.text: Draw on prior knowledge of texts to question, challenge and deepen understanding of both new and familiar texts
Clarify and justify personal responses to texts, explaining how aspects of the text, such as character, genre, tone, salience or voice, position a reader and influence these personal responses
Analyse how the use of language forms and features in texts have the capacity to create multiple meanings
Analyse how language use evolves over time and is influenced by social and technological changes and developments
items.examples: Understanding how the use of language influences how we create different identities, and how online platforms have adopted or created particular words or ways of speaking.

contentGroups.title: Reading for challenge, interest and enjoyment

items.text: Read increasingly complex texts that challenge thinking, pique interest, enhance enjoyment and provoke a personal response

Engage in sustained and varied reading that presents increasingly diverse and complex perspectives and experiences, including those of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, and respond in a range of ways, including through extended written responses
items.examples: Participating in sustained and independent reading, using multiple cognitive processes, such as making inferences, identifying connections and monitoring understanding.

items.text: Consider how the social, cultural and ethical positions represented in texts represent, affirm or challenge views of the world
Evaluate experiences of reading by sharing responses to texts
Evaluate the ways reading texts help us understand ourselves and make connections to others and the world
Reflect on how reading, viewing and listening to texts has informed and inspired learning
Reflect on how an appreciation of texts can be enhanced through re-reading, and close or critical study
Understand and reflect on the value of reading for personal growth and cultural richness
Use reading strategies, and evaluate their effectiveness, when reflecting on the successes and challenges of extended reading
Reflect on how reading promotes a broad and balanced understanding of the world and enables students to explore wider universal issues
Reflect on own experiences of reading by interacting with peers in meaningful ways about the value of reading

focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to texts B

outcomes.description: evaluates how texts represent ideas and experiences, and how they can affirm or challenge values and attitudes

items.text: Analyse how themes can be understood to underpin cohesive meaning in texts, and apply this understanding in own texts
Appreciate the role of the audience in perceiving themes and how these themes can offer insights into an author’s perspective
Understand how the personal perspectives of audiences are a product of historical and cultural contexts
Analyse how texts can be understood or interpreted from different perspectives, and experiment with this idea in own texts
Evaluate how texts can position audiences to accept, challenge or reject particular perspectives of the world, and reflect on this in own texts
Analyse how elements of an author’s personal, cultural and political contexts can shape their perspectives and representation of ideas, including form and purpose
items.examples: Researching the literary context of a text and using this information to interpret how ideas have been depicted.

items.text: Appreciate how all communication is a product of cultural context
items.examples: Engaging with a selection of narratives, poetry and artworks by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors, and discussing how words and images are used to reflect connections to Country/Place.

items.text: Explain how texts affirm or challenge established cultural attitudes and values in different contexts

Appreciate the significance and value of expressions of cultural context in texts constructed using elements of languages and dialects, including Standard Australian English, Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Languages, and Aboriginal English
items.examples: Considering how the use of words from specific languages can describe, represent and pass on cultural knowledge and ways of thinking about experiences.

items.text: Evaluate how effective arguments are constructed through combinations of specific language forms, features and structures, and apply an understanding of this in own texts
Analyse how subjectivity and objectivity are constructed in texts to form arguments, and how these can represent particular perspectives
items.examples:
Reshaping a subjective extract to create an objective voice.

Examining an auteur’s work and analysing how their typical aesthetic and use of structural features construct mood and theme across multiple texts.

items.text: Analyse how an engaging personal voice in texts can represent a perspective or argument and communicate a sense of authority, and experiment with these ideas in own texts
Research, select and sequence appropriate evidence from texts and reliable sources to construct cohesive and authoritative arguments
Evaluate how the authority of a text is continually negotiated and reassessed by readers
items.examples: Examining 2 texts that present conflicting perspectives on an issue and considering how the second text challenges the authority of the first.

items.text: Appreciate how authority over meaning in texts, such as multimodal and interactive texts, can be distributed, and is a negotiation between acts of authorship, publication and interpretation
items.examples:
Exploring how digital advertising can use algorithms across connected platforms to gather personal data from the audience and tailor published content of the text, considering how a user’s unconscious contribution of data contributes to, or subverts, the authority of the text.

Examining how digital texts, such as video games, can offer users interactive control in directing or constructing characters and narratives.

items.text: Analyse how the distinctive aesthetic qualities and stylistic features of a text can shape and be shaped by its purpose, and experiment with this in own texts
Evaluate how particular styles in text can be privileged according to context
Examine the way an author’s distinct personal style shapes meaning in their work
Appreciate how the style of a text can represent larger ideas of literary movements and genres
items.examples: Explaining how a poem from the Romantic movement draws on stylistic elements typical of its time, including heightened narrative drama, natural settings, and thematic focuses on ideas such as love and struggle.

focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to texts B

outcomes.description: identifies ideas, experiences and values in a range of texts

items.text: Recognise that texts convey messages
items.examples:
Identifying social or moral issues or dilemmas in texts.

Exploring characters or events in a narrative and discussing what the characters have taught us.

items.text: Explore and communicate ideas and information in texts
items.examples:
Answering yes/no questions based on a text.

Re-telling ideas or information in a text, using pictures or words.

Summarising a topic in short sentences.

items.text: Explore the messages, values or experiences in texts
items.examples: Identifying ways that an Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander author represents a character’s connection to Country/Place.

items.text: Explore home languages and language connections within the class or community
items.examples: Creating a presentation of home languages and/or cultural backgrounds of peers.

items.text: Explore representations of cultures and traditions in texts
items.examples: Recognising cultural practices presented in a film and comparing these with their own cultural practices.

items.text: Recognise that languages and dialects, including Standard Australian English, Auslan, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages, and Aboriginal English, can represent expressions of cultural context within texts
items.examples: Recognising culturally specific language in texts by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander authors, such as Uncle, Aunty or tidda.

items.text: Recognise that an author’s personal and cultural experiences can shape meaning in a text
items.examples:
Identifying the perspective, voice and/or personal and cultural background of an author.

Communicating how an author’s experience has shaped meaning in a text.

items.text: Explore how culture and identity influence perspectives in texts
items.examples:
Exploring how diverse cultures may have different perspectives of the same events.

Communicating a story from different perspectives.

items.text: Respond to a text by providing a justified opinion of their own perspective
items.examples:
Responding with an opinion that may include I like, I do not like or I feel.

Communicating an opinion online in a constructive manner.

items.text: Identify fact and opinion in texts
items.examples: Exploring newspaper editorials, advertisements, sports results, blogs or posters to identify fact or opinion.

items.text: Identify an intended meaning of a text
Select and use evidence to support an argument
items.examples:
Identifying a character in a text as the hero and justifying this using the character’s actions as evidence.

Finding data in an informative text to use when creating a persuasive text.

items.text: Identify an authoritative voice in a text
items.examples: Identifying features that create authority in informative texts, such as technical vocabulary, grammar, quotations and references.

items.text: Identify elements of style in a text
items.examples: Identifying visual or linguistic elements.

items.text: Recognise the purpose of different texts by their style
items.examples: Differentiating between a brochure, a newspaper article, a vlog, a poem or a narrative.

items.text: Explore how elements of style have been used to communicate ideas, experiences and values
items.examples:
Exploring visual elements of texts and how these are used to reinforce an idea, experience or value in a text.

Identifying the tone of a text from word choices and connecting this to how the author wants us to feel about an idea or experience.

Recognising language features, such as description, symbolism and figurative language, and what this communicates about an idea, experience or value.

items.text: Compare texts and identify how style changes according to audience or purpose
items.examples: Engaging with advertisements for the same product in different contexts and understanding how the audience affects the stylistic choices.

focusAreas.title: Understanding and responding to texts C

outcomes.description: investigates and explains ways of valuing texts and the relationships between them

items.text: Analyse how elements of genre in texts can shape the way ideas and values are represented and perceived, and experiment with elements of genre in own texts to shape meaning and response
Reflect on the evolution, adaptation, subversion and hybridity of genre in different time periods and cultural contexts, and how they demonstrate changing values
items.examples: Investigating different adaptations of novels into films to explore how changing values are reflected in the evolution of thematic representation, style and form.

items.text: Identify the process and value of adapting, appropriating or transforming texts for different audiences, purposes or contexts, and describe these processes in own texts
items.examples: Comparing a classic novel with a contemporary re-telling of the same story and evaluating how effectively the new version adapts elements of the original for a modern audience.

items.text: Examine how meaningful connections made between texts can enrich the experience and understanding of literature and culture
Analyse and evaluate how thematic and aesthetic qualities of a text contribute to the different ways an audience questions and negotiates the value of the text in particular contexts
items.examples: Examining a classic novel and comparing how its depiction of particular ideas was received at the time of publication and how this has shifted over time.

focusAreas.title: Communicating

outcomes.description: communicates in familiar or unfamiliar contexts

items.text: Respond to familiar or unfamiliar people, auditory signals and cues in their environment
items.examples:
Demonstrating a head turn, nod, smile or following a signal in response to a cue.

Responding to the teacher’s voice or to their name.

Responding to announcements, the school bell, fire or smoke alarms.

items.text: Recognise nonverbal indicators associated with communication
items.examples:
Nonverbal indicators may include eye contact, nodding, smiling, gesturing, turning away, frowning or other modalities of communication.

Identifying the emotions of a character in a visual text through their body language.

Responding appropriately to a gesture to indicate stop.

items.text: Respond to environmental cues and language with increased self-regulation
items.examples:
Opening their lunchbox and selecting food during lunchtime.

Responding appropriately to beeps at pedestrian lights, sirens, the telephone or announcements on public transport.

Demonstrating communication etiquette in different settings, such as using a quiet voice inside.

items.text: Follow single or multistep instructions
items.examples:
Responding to the phrases stop, wait, look or turn the page.

Responding to routine multistep instructions, such as 'check the schedule and tell me what you see', or ‘stay with the group and teacher’.

Navigating to a page of a written text, or timestamp of a film.

items.text: Express or communicate basic needs, wants, preferences or choices
items.examples:
Seeking permission, indicating a like or dislike, or continuing or ceasing an activity.

Using language to express requests in a social or community setting.

Expressing a preference for a particular genre of text.

Identifying a preferred character and expressing reasons for this choice.

items.text: Communicate in response to other people initiating a dialogue
items.examples:
Responding appropriately when greeted.

Answering a question.

items.text: Engage in simple interactions, discussions or responses to questions
items.examples:
Giving their name to a teacher or making a comment in a conversation.

Responding to an online comment or post.

items.text: Initiate an interaction in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
items.examples:
Using eye gaze or gesture to select an activity or request information.

Asking an unfamiliar person a question.

Seeking clarification.

Participating in a group activity.

items.text: Recognise different forms of communication
items.examples:
Engaging with actions, images, photographs, gestures, symbols, Key Word Sign and spoken language as forms of communication.

Identifying how elements of film production, such as colour and music, are used to communicate meaning.

Engaging with a telephone, text, letter, email, online forum, film, media and/or the internet to communicate.

items.text: Communicate emotions and feelings in contextually appropriate ways
